name: Yugoslavia
summary: A state of South Slavs created in 1918; under Tito (1945–80) a non-aligned communist federation; it broke apart in the wars of the 1990s.
borderNames: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes

knownFor.label: Non-Aligned Movement
knownFor.note: Founded in Belgrade by Tito, Nehru, Nasser and others.

location.value: Central Europe and the Balkans (1918–92). The page gives no total area, only the areas of the successor states.

terrain.value: Mountains, the Adriatic coast, the Pannonian plain.

climate.value: Mediterranean on the Adriatic coast, and continental in the north and in the inland mountains.

resources.value: Farmland, copper, bauxite, coal and tourism on the Adriatic coast.

disasters.value: The Skopje earthquake of 1963 killed over 1,000 people and destroyed most of the city.

urbanisation.value: Belgrade (the capital), Zagreb, Sarajevo, Ljubljana and Skopje were the main cities.

disease.value: Health care was good for its income level, with free care for citizens.

migration.value: Many worked in West Germany as guest workers.

economicBase.value: Official statistics show rapid growth from the 1950s to the early 1980s; growth then stalled after the 1970s oil shock, heavy foreign borrowing caused a debt problem, and hundreds of thousands were laid off in 1989–90. Tourism and workers’ self-management are not mentioned in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: It traded with both the Soviet bloc and the West, and Adriatic ports such as Rijeka and Split served trade.

wealth.value: A middle-income country, with large gaps between rich northern republics and poorer southern ones.

inequality.value: Gaps between richer north and poorer south.

governmentType.value: Formed in 1918 as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and renamed Yugoslavia on 3 October 1929; proclaimed a federal republic on 29 November 1945; renamed the Socialist Federal Republic on 7 April 1963, when Tito was made president for life.

keyRulers.value: Tito ruled from 1944 until his death on 4 May 1980; the country was renamed the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1963.

succession.value: After 1945 the Communist Party ruled; Tito led until his death in 1980, then a rotating presidency took over.

institutions.value: Six republics and two autonomous provinces.

stability.value: Occupied and torn by war (1941–45); broke up in 1991–92.

eliteConflict.value: Rival national republics after Tito’s death.

armyAndTech.value: The Yugoslav People’s Army was among the largest in Europe, with a strong tradition from the Partisan war.

majorWars.value: The Axis powers invaded and occupied the kingdom in April 1941.

territoryChange.value: Broke apart from 1991–92 into Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia and Bosnia, with Serbia and Montenegro continuing a smaller Yugoslavia.

alliancesRivals.value: Non-aligned after the break with Stalin in 1948, Yugoslavia balanced between East and West.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded for the state itself.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy rose strongly after 1945, with free schooling and many new universities.

openness.value: More open than the Soviet bloc, with relatively free travel abroad and some market features.

communicationTransport.value: Railways and the “Highway of Brotherhood and Unity” linked Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade and Skopje; the Adriatic road ran along the coast.

religion.value: A 1964 survey found just over 70% considered themselves believers; the state was de facto atheist, though the Catholic Church and the Serbian Orthodox Church stayed active. Muslim communities are not covered in the part of the page read.

languageWriting.value: Serbo-Croatian (Latin and Cyrillic scripts), Slovene and Macedonian, plus Albanian and Hungarian in some regions.

artsArchitecture.value: Ivo Andrić won the Nobel Prize in 1961; Belgrade’s brutalist buildings and Mostar’s old bridge are famous.

socialStructure.value: A varied society of workers, peasants and an educated middle class, divided among six republics.

dailyLife.value: Many people lived in apartment blocks and ate ćevapi, burek and cabbage rolls.

neighbours.value: Italy, Austria, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, Albania.

ideasReligions.value: Non-alignment, workers’ self-management and “brotherhood and unity” were the main state ideas.

colonisation.value: None; it did not hold overseas colonies.

riseSignals.value: Created on 1 December 1918 as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes; King Alexander I renamed it Yugoslavia in 1929.

peakPeriod.value: The page gives no peak; it shows rapid growth from the 1950s to the early 1980s, a wider span than the entry’s 1960s–70s.

declineSignals.value: Economic crisis and nationalism in the 1980s.

outcome.value: The federation broke up along republic borders into five countries and the Yugoslav Wars followed; the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was formed on 27 April 1992, renamed Serbia and Montenegro in 2003 and dissolved in 2006.
